title: Medellín (1968)
hookLine: Latin American bishops commit to the poor

lines: WHAT SHOULD THE CHURCH LOOK LIKE?
cards: A city in the mountains of Colombia, and a meeting room full of bishops from across Latin America. Outside, their continent: grand cathedrals, and not far from the cathedral steps, families with very little.
The question on the table was simple to ask and hard to answer. What should the Church look like in a place like this? Rich and distant, or close enough to share the same street?
The documents they wrote there are known by the city's name. Today's word is Medellín.

teach.h: ANOINTED TO PREACH TO THE POOR.
teach.b: First, a text that sits close to their concern. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus reads from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth.

In the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Read beside Medellín, it sounds like a description of the Church's job, not only of Jesus's.
Their document on the poverty of the Church names three senses. Poverty as lack: not enough food, housing, schooling. That, they say, is an evil, and not something God wants.
Spiritual poverty: an open, empty-handed trust in God, the poverty of the beatitudes.
And poverty as a commitment: choosing, freely and out of love, to share the condition of the poor, to stand with them and work against what keeps them poor. Third, the turn toward themselves.

The bishops asked their own Church to live more simply, to make its buildings, titles and ways of living plainer, and to be present where the poor are. Not a Church that hands things down to the poor from a height.

teach.h: NOT FOR THE POOR, BUT WITH THEM.
teach.b: A Church with the poor. Fourth, why it reaches past Latin America. Some readers trace the phrase from last week, the option for the poor, back to soil like this.
Whatever the history, the shape works on any ordinary day: tell apart the poverty to fight, the poverty to welcome, and the poverty to choose.

how: Many Catholic communities in Latin America and beyond draw on the Medellín documents in their work with the poor, through base communities, parish outreach and religious orders living in poor neighborhoods.

games.q: you're a bishop at Medellín. the cathedral is grand and the streets around it are poor. what do you commit to?
o: keep things as they are and send help from a distance.
a Church that lives simply and stands with the poor.
leave the question of poverty to governments.
games.why: the bishops asked for a poorer Church, present among the poor, living out what Jesus reads in Luke 4:18: good news to the poor.

practice: Picture the map, Mexico down through Central America, the islands, the long sweep of South America to its tip, and let a few names come: a city, a country, someone you know with family there.
Then let faces come: the street vendor, the grandmother raising grandchildren, the priest or nun working in a poor barrio.
If you pray, hold that whole continent before God, in Spanish or Portuguese if you know a prayer; if you don't, simply wish them well, one place at a time.

wordCard.voice: Medellín. The Colombian city where Latin American bishops met and committed the Church to stand with the poor, and to become poorer itself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: with the poor. Alongside them, never above them, on the same street. Until tomorrow.
